title: Video upload pipeline
like: uploads on a site like YouTube
brief: Creators upload videos that must be converted into several qualities before anyone can watch. Conversion is slow, costs real money per video, and the converter sometimes fails on a broken file. Nothing a creator uploads can be lost.

clarify.q: Must the creator wait while the video converts?
clarify.a: No. The upload is accepted right away. The video shows as "processing" and goes live when ready, within about ten minutes.

clarify.q: What if the same upload is sent twice because the connection dropped?
clarify.a: It must not be converted twice. Each conversion costs about a dollar.

clarify.q: What if one file is corrupted?
clarify.a: It will fail every time. It must not block the other uploads behind it.

clarify.q: What if the converter service is down for a while?
clarify.a: Uploads still succeed and wait in line. They convert once it comes back.

requirements.users: 8 million viewers a month, 15 thousand uploads a day
notes: Converting one 10-minute video into five qualities costs about $1 at list price (approx.). Conversion is the largest line on the bill.
One upload request in the game stands for one whole video handed over to be converted.

hints: The converter is slow, costly and sometimes broken. What goes between the upload and the converter?

A queue accepts the upload at once and hands videos to the converter at its own pace. A dead-letter queue catches the file that keeps failing. An idempotency store stops a repeated upload from converting twice.
Try: creators -> app servers -> object storage (save the file first) -> queue -> workflow engine -> video transcoder, with a dead-letter queue beside the queue. Viewers read through a CDN.

editorial.summary: Save the file first, then do the slow work later. Object storage keeps the original safe. A queue and workflow engine turn each upload into a job that survives a converter outage. A dead-letter queue isolates the one broken file. An idempotency store makes a repeated upload cost nothing. Viewing sits on a separate path through the CDN.

designs.name: Save first, convert later
designs.why: The upload is acknowledged once its job is safely in the queue, which keeps it durably until it is converted. The queue and workflow engine feed the converter at its own pace and keep jobs during an outage. Broken files go to a dead-letter queue instead of blocking everything. Viewers never touch the upload path.

tradeoffs: Accepting the upload before converting means a creator sees "processing" for minutes, but the upload never fails because the converter is slow.
Retrying a failed conversion fixes temporary problems but wastes money on a broken file. A retry limit plus a dead-letter queue stops that.
Keeping the original forever lets you convert again to a better format later, but originals are big and cost storage every month.
Converting only the qualities people actually watch cuts the largest line on the bill, but the first viewer of a rare quality waits.
Idempotency keys cost one fast lookup per upload and save a dollar every time a connection drops.
editorial.realWorld: Video sites receive hundreds of hours of new video per minute in total (approx.). Conversion is done by large pools of dedicated workers fed from queues, and failed jobs are retried a few times, then parked for a person to look at.
